title: Balanced Scorecard
hook: The exam loves to hand you a target ("cut defects", "grow repeat sales") and ask which of the 4 BSC perspectives it belongs to.
model: A **Balanced Scorecard (BSC)** translates strategy into 4 linked perspectives: **Financial**, **Customer**, **Internal business process**, **Learning & growth**.
Each perspective pairs a *strategic target* with a *KPI* (key performance indicator) that measures progress toward it.
**Financial**: targets like profitability/growth \n KPI examples: ROI, revenue growth.
**Customer**: targets like satisfaction/retention \n KPI examples: repeat-purchase rate, complaint count.
**Internal business process**: targets like efficiency/quality inside operations \n KPI examples: defect rate, manufacturing lead time.
**Learning & growth**: targets like employee capability/innovation \n KPI examples: training hours, skill certification rate.

example.q: A factory wants to cut the number of days it takes to manufacture a unit. Which perspective and KPI fit?
steps: Ask what the target describes: doing the work faster/better _{inside operations}_, not selling or external relations.
That points to the **internal business process** perspective.
A matching KPI: reduction in **manufacturing lead time** (days from start to finished unit).
Check it isn't customer-facing (no complaints/satisfaction mentioned) or financial (no cost/revenue figure) — confirms internal business process.

checks.q: Match each BSC perspective to an example strategic target/KPI pair.
checks.why: Each KPI is defined by what it measures: ROI measures money (financial), complaint rate measures how customers feel (customer), defect rate measures how the operation runs (internal process), and certification rate measures staff capability (learning & growth).

checks.q: Arrange the four BSC perspectives in the order they're usually drawn, top to bottom.
checks.why: The classic Kaplan & Norton diagram stacks Financial on top (the ultimate goal), then Customer, then Internal business process, then Learning & growth at the base (the capability that enables everything above it).

checks.q: A hospital shortens the average time a patient waits between check-in and seeing a doctor. Which perspective does this target belong to?
checks.why: Wait time between steps of a workflow is an operational-efficiency measure — it's about how the process runs, not a cost/revenue figure (financial) or a training measure (learning & growth).

trap: Don't confuse a customer-facing *outcome* (e.g., a satisfaction score) with an internal *process* metric (e.g., cycle time) just because the process serves the customer — the perspective is defined by what is measured, not by who ultimately benefits.

title: Earned Value Management (EVM)
hook: EVM questions give you three dollar figures and ask whether the project is over budget, behind schedule, or both — you just need the right formula.
model: **PV** (Planned Value): the budgeted cost of the work that was *scheduled* to be done by now.
**EV** (Earned Value): the budgeted cost of the work *actually completed* so far.
**AC** (Actual Cost): the real money *spent* on the work done so far.
**CV** (Cost Variance) = `EV − AC`. Positive means under budget; negative means over budget.
**SV** (Schedule Variance) = `EV − PV`. Positive means ahead of schedule; negative means behind schedule.
**CPI** = `EV / AC` and **SPI** = `EV / PV`. Values above 1 are good (efficient); below 1 are bad.

example.q: A project's PV to date is `$100,000`, EV is `$90,000`, and AC is `$120,000`. How is the project doing?
steps: CPI = EV / AC = 90,000 / 120,000 = **0.75** (every $1 spent earns only $0.75 of planned value).
SPI = EV / PV = 90,000 / 100,000 = **0.9** (progressing at 90% of the planned pace).
Both variances are negative and both indices are below 1: the project is over budget _and_ behind schedule.

checks.q: Match each EVM term to its definition.
pairs: Budgeted cost of the work scheduled to be done by now
Budgeted cost of the work actually completed so far
Actual cost spent on the work completed so far
checks.why: PV is the plan, EV is the budget value of what's actually done, and AC is the real money spent getting it done — three separate measurements taken at the same point in time.

checks.q: A task has PV = `$50,000` and EV = `$42,000`. What is the schedule variance (SV), in dollars? (negative if behind schedule)
checks.why: SV = EV − PV = 42,000 − 50,000 = **−$8,000**. A negative SV means the work completed so far is worth less than what was scheduled — the project is behind schedule.

checks.q: A project has AC = `$80,000` and EV = `$80,000`. Which measure tells you directly whether the project is on schedule — not just on budget?
checks.why: SPI = EV/PV compares earned value to *planned* value, which is a schedule measure. CPI and CV both compare EV to AC, which measures cost performance, not schedule.

trap: Don't mix up CV and SV: both use EV as the baseline, but CV compares it to AC (cost) while SV compares it to PV (schedule). A negative SV does **not** mean over budget — it means behind schedule; check CV separately for budget status.
